I'm hoping Ben (or someone else) can help sort me out on this.

I added a data type for a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix.
It's all pushed to this branch:

  feature/issue-413-cholesky-corr-type

It all seems to work.  For unit tests, I checked that autodiff on
the transform followed by a direct determinant calc gives the same
answer as the transform Jacobian (it does) and that the values round
trip back and forth properly under the constrain/free transforms (they do).

The problem I'm left with is conceptual, and it's also left me worried
about correlation matrices.

Consider this trivial model:

  parameters {
    cholesky_factor_corr[4] L;
  }
  model {
  }
  generated quantities {
    matrix[4,4] Omega;
    Omega <- L * L';
  }

The fit is consistently this (under different seeds, longer warmup, etc.):

                      Mean     MCSE   StdDev     5%       50%    95%  N_Eff  N_Eff/s    R_hat
  Omega[2,1]       3.0e-04  4.1e-03  5.8e-01  -0.90   1.1e-03   0.90  19478     7569  1.0e+00
  Omega[3,1]       8.6e-04  3.5e-03  5.0e-01  -0.81   2.6e-03   0.80  19754     7676  1.0e+00
  Omega[3,2]      -1.1e-04  3.6e-03  5.0e-01  -0.81  -2.0e-04   0.80  19731     7667  1.0e+00
  Omega[4,1]      -1.1e-03  3.2e-03  4.5e-01  -0.73  -4.0e-03   0.73  20000     7772  1.0e+00
  Omega[4,2]      -3.8e-03  3.2e-03  4.5e-01  -0.74  -8.1e-03   0.73  20000     7772  1.0e+00
  Omega[4,3]      -8.5e-04  3.2e-03  4.5e-01  -0.73  -1.1e-03   0.73  20000     7772  1.0e+00

The means and medians are OK (should be 0, I believe), but the 90% intervals are not the same for
the six correlation entries.  My understanding is that these should all be identical, as each is just
a pairwise correlation.

But then I realized that there's no reason to suppose that just because L is drawn uniformly
from the Cholesky factors for correlation matrices that (L * L') will thus be uniform over
correlation matrices --- it's missing the product-transpose Jacobian!

But then I tried looking at what we get just from correlation matrices, using an even more trivial
model:

  parameters {
    corr_matrix[4] Omega;
  }
  model {
  }

and got:

                      Mean     MCSE   StdDev     5%       50%    95%  N_Eff  N_Eff/s    R_hat
  Omega[2,1]      -5.3e-03  3.2e-03  4.5e-01  -0.74  -7.1e-03   0.74  19718     5851  1.0e+00
  Omega[3,1]       3.0e-03  3.2e-03  4.5e-01  -0.73   1.4e-03   0.74  19948     5919  1.0e+00
  Omega[3,2]       3.6e-04  2.9e-03  4.1e-01  -0.67   2.7e-03   0.67  19724     5853  1.0e+00
  Omega[4,1]       1.2e-03  3.2e-03  4.5e-01  -0.73   2.8e-03   0.73  19148     5682  1.0e+00
  Omega[4,2]      -8.1e-04  2.9e-03  4.1e-01  -0.67  -3.9e-03   0.67  20000     5935  1.0e+00
  Omega[4,3]       7.4e-04  3.2e-03  4.5e-01  -0.73   4.0e-03   0.73  19601     5816  1.0e+00

repeats under all conditions I can find (and is reflected in the StdDev values varying, too).

So my question is whether this is OK and I'm just testing or conceptualizing improperly.

The second question is whether the right thing to do is write:

   cholesky_factor_corr[K] L;
   L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(nu);

Will that produce the lkj_corr distribution on (L * L')?

messages.body_plain:
Ben will have to give the definition answer, but I think you have
a misinterpretation here.

In the LKJ construction the off-diagonal elements of the Cholesky
matrix are partial (i.e. conditional) correlations, not the pairwise
covariances/correlations of the resulting covariance/correlation matrix.
Think about it this way: the LKJ prior is just the determinant of
the covariance matrix raised to some power, but the determinant
is given entirely by the diagonal elements of the Cholesky factor.
The off diagonal elements are completely unconstrained by the
prior!

I’m not sure about the correlation matrix, but I’m also not sure that
it’s wrong.  The 0.67 values are the off-diagonal elements of the
second row, which is the central row of the lower triangle (4x4 matrix,
4 diagonal elements, 6 elements forming a triangle below the diagonal
and 6 elements forming a triangle above the diagonal).  This seems
structured enough to be consistent with an implicit prior given by the
squared Jacobian alone.

The correlations only have the same marginal distribution under the LKJ(1) prior on the correlation matrix, which isn't achieved by a uniform prior on L.

> But then I realized that there's no reason to suppose that just because L is drawn uniformly
> from the Cholesky factors for correlation matrices that (L * L') will thus be uniform over
> correlation matrices --- it's missing the product-transpose Jacobian!

Right. This is going to be a challenge to get users to recognize that they must put a non-uniform prior on L in order to imply a uniform (or even non-uniform LKJ) prior on L * L' when L * L' is typically not even constructed in their model.

I'm not sure what is going on there. It should be .73. More generally when eta = 1, the marginal distribution of each correlation should be that of

2 * b - 1

where b is distributed beta with both shape parameters equal to K / 2.

> The second question is whether the right thing to do is write:
>
>    cholesky_factor_corr[K] L;
>    L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(nu);
>
> Will that produce the lkj_corr distribution on (L * L')?

That is probably the right behavior, but I need to rewrite the lkj_corr_cholesky_log function to achieve it. The density of L can be expressed as

|J| * det(L)^(2 * eta - 2)

and that J is triangular with diagonal elements that only involve powers of the diagonal of L.

Ben

That's where we're going with the relationship between Stan and its interfaces. Right now, we've (almost) got the system set up for CmdStan. After the refactoring effort I'm going through, we'll have RStan going too.

> >

That is true, but it works slightly differently than that. For the development branch of CmdStan, we are going to be compatible to the current version of Stan.

That is false. The minimum number of pull requests needed is 1: one per tagged version of Stan.

Exactly. So the way it works now is, work on Stan, commit, submit a pull request. If you're working on core Stan, you won't be affecting the interfaces; we'll test through the interface(s) just to make sure things are compatible. (We have this issue now where the pull request made on Stan doesn't propagate through the CmdStan's submodule of Stan, but hopefully we can fix that... the temporary fix is to create a branch on Stan that has the changes and the pull requests will go through).

If the pull request actually stops CmdStan, RStan, or *Stan from building, that should not go into Stan as-is. I'm going to be adamant about that. The last thing we want is for developers not to trust the current state of any of the interfaces because it's out of synch.

Do we want to introduce the non-square cholesky_factor_corr[R,C] with R >= C type now? The main use I could see for that is the matrix of coefficients in models with continuous latent predictors. In general, you can multiply the coefficients by any square matrix and multiply the predictors by the inverse of that matrix without changing the likelihood. Some people use a cholesky_factor_cov[R,C] for the coefficients, but you can still multiply the coefficients by a diagonal matrix with positive diagonal elements and multiply the predictors by the inverse of that matrix without changing the likelihood. But if the rows were normalized to have unit length as they would be with a cholesky_factor_corr[R,C] type, then anything you multiply by except the identity matrix would violate the constraint.

messages.subject: Re: example of flaky chain
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, March 11, 2014 9:16:59 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> I don't know if we need a separate repo, but there is no great shortage of flaky BUGS examples. All of these were for 21 chains with a base seed of 12345 that is advanced by the chain_id but otherwise kept the default settings
>
> Stan doesn't parse: fire
> Stan blows up: salm2, salm, orange
> Stan takes way too long: schools (not eight_schools)
> Stan doesn't converge: hepatitisME, hepatitis, air, eyes
> Stan has bad mixing at a minimum: blocker, kidney, leukfr, magnesium, seeds, birats, stagnant
>
> In each of these cases (except fire), the model wasn't much better with JAGS, so I think it is more a situation where the models are bad (gamma(0,0) priors, etc.). And it underscores that these BUGS examples are not good for unit-testing, but it would be nice if Stan could do a little better.

There is a discussion on stan-users about the blocker example in volume 1 of BUGS. Whether you get reasonable results depends on the seed, number of chains, number of iterations, etc., which is to say I don't think that Stan gives reasonable results. With these arguments:
library(rstan)
blocker <- stan_demo("blocker", seed = 12345, chains = 21, iter = 10000)

you get low Rhat values for all quantities
> summary(summary(blocker)$summary[,"Rhat"])
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
  1.000   1.001   1.001   1.002   1.002   1.010

but chain 6, for example, does not mix well (see the clump below the diagonal)
pairs(blocker, pars = c("d", "delta_new", "sigma_delta", "lp__"), chain_id = list(6, c(1:5,7:21)))

 <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-RWdBi_6eUCA/U2ljvedR43I/AAAAAAAAAPw/daj4WxmRDOc/s1600/pairs_blocker.png>
Hopefully a user would notice that the ratio of n_eff to nm is low for several parameters, but a more concise way of saying it is that it takes at least 20 lags for the draws to become essentially independent (and it looks like the adaptation was thrown off somewhat):

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-OY7ia_6LGBc/U2ll2OvUZyI/AAAAAAAAAP8/4CMZUh9Xwc8/s1600/dependence_blocker.png>
Finally, you would reject the null hypothesis that all the chains have the same distribution, which is appropriate in light of chain 6:
> convergence(blocker, thin = 25, R = 199)
[1] "Multivariate loss = 1.004"
disco(x = mat, factors = chain_id, distance = FALSE, R = R)

Distance Components: index  1.00
Source                 Df   Sum Dist  Mean Dist    F-ratio    p-value
factors                41  543.49225   13.25591      1.865      0.005
Within               4158 29555.97387    7.10822
Total                4199 30099.46612

There are some mitigating circumstances (it's a bad model, many of the chains seem fine, BUGS gets similar results, etc.) but this isn't great.

Ben

I'm glad Allen spoke up about PyStan's implementation.

I didn't realize C++ was part of the issue and we might be able to solve it if we were to provide a reasonable C API. (I should have, since I'm deep in RStan code, but I've had blinders on for the last month.) I'm guessing that R, Python, and Julia aren't the only potential interfaces that would benefit from having C bindings exposed. Would that solve problem 1?

Pros:
- RStan would no longer need to depend on Rcpp
- PyStan wouldn't need the Cython dependency? (I think Python can call C functions directly; Allen, can you confirm?)
- Stan.jl would be easy to write.

Cons:
- the work in figuring out how to do it
- additional maintenance

> As Bob stated in an earlier email, some of the Rstan functionality is being moved into C++ for performance reasons.

I think the underlying reason is to reduce duplication of code and effort. We are trying to bring more of the shared logic across interfaces into Stan itself and reduce the footprint of each of our interfaces. Ideally, each interface would be a simple wrapper, implementing a handful of functions dealing mostly with I/O from the appropriate interface. (Those functions won't all be trivial, but it'll all be specific to the interaction of the interface with Stan.) This will also allow us to keep things in synch across different interfaces. If functionality is implemented in RStan, CmdStan, and PyStan independently, to squash a bug, it needs to be killed in each of those places. I'd rather they all call the same function, fail the same way, and get fixed the same way.

Unfortunately, we didn't start that way and it'll be some time before this happens, especially since we have existing, working implementations. I'm treading very, very lightly in my refactoring effort.

> My question is, will there be, from the general design point of view, a command line equivalent for such functionality, e.g. in Bob's earlier email the monitor() capability? Would it be possible, where applicable, to optionally capture these results in a file? Or could this be achieved through the new function feature in the modeling language? Yes to all? I think?

>

Clearly this can be done on the Julia side as well, but it would always have to stay in sync with changes in Stan. Having access to the gradients and maybe in the future to higher order derivatives might help comparisons with AD technology in Julia.

The refactoring effort that was merged in this week gives the ability to record the unconstrained and constrained values, if desired. So we're already going down that path. And keeping things in synch with changes to Stan is exactly why I've gone down this path.

But my guess is that for folks that come from other technical computing platforms (R, Matlab, Fortran libraries), this is not the case even though many might at least occasionally use the IJulia interface.

Sorry, I'm lost on this point. Did you want IJulia to handle Stan? Perhaps some background would help me understand the question / point.

> 4) Installing/updating CmdStan.
>
> I'm not planning to attack this area at this point in time as it is very much in flux (CMake, stan as a submodule). Longer term I would like to see if it is possible to bring it into the Julia fold by using Julia's version of homebrew.

> Today, if I understand Daniel's emails correctly, to update CmdStan and the stan submodule in an existing cmdstan source directory, one runs:
>
> git pull https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan develop

That's pretty much it. If you clone CmdStan directly from GitHub, it doesn't automatically grab the Stan submodule.

>From the cmdstan directory, "make stan-update" will setup the submodule and grab a copy of Stan if you don't already have it setup.
"make stan-update/<branch>" will update that submodule to the latest version of that branch (or SHA). You can also manipulate the Stan submodule directory by changing into that directory and updating branches, etc.
"make stan-revert" is going to drop changes in the Stan submodule and return it to the state of the current CmdStan branch.

"make clean-all" gets rid of all the artifacts. This is useful when the libs are built using some other version of the Stan submodule, etc.

Instead of making bin/libstan.a and bin/stanc, you could alternative just type "make build -j4" and that should build bin/stanc and bin/print. Or continue to do what you do. Either will work.

> (While testing I found out inserting the 'make clean-all' step prevents, in some cases, crashes later on when running stan.)

Yeah, that can happen with incompatible libs.

Awesome! Have you taken a look at PyMC?

I've got a few more random thoughts, but I think I should edit them into complete ideas before shooting them off.

messages.body_plain:
[now on stan-dev]

Two embedded questions.

On May 13, 2014, at 1:04 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Hi, Bob.  Where do these names fabs, fmin, fmax, etc come from? Why not abs, min, max?

They come from the standard C++ library, which uses "f" for
floating point to distinguish them from their equivalent integer
versions.  So you have built into C++:

  real fabs(real);

  int abs(int);

But then C++ will also promote int to real and vice-versa, so you also
get:

  real fabs(int);

  int abs(real);

Stan only allows promotion of int to real, not the other way around (in this,
it's like Java, not like C++).

Right now, using abs(real) in Stan is deprecated and issues a warning.

Issue 1
-------

I think we should go 180 on this and instead add the following signatures
with obvious definitions:

  real abs(real);

  real max(real,real);
  real max(real, int);
  real max(int, real);

We already have:

  int abs(int);
  int max(int, int);

Is that OK with everyone?

Issue 2
-------

Do we deprecate and eventually get rid of the f versions?  I don't see
the point of keeping them.  I don't really see anyone wanting to do
fabs(int,int), which is all we'd be losing.  Anywhere you can use a real
value in Stan you can use an int.

- Bob

We've had requests for marginalizing out unbounded discrete
params in Poisson-like models.

I'm hoping we can go some way to supporting R-like missing data
input without actually ripping the guts of Stan apart in terms
of data types.

I'm not talking about setting up a database per se, so much as
using data-structure-like representations.  R users might be
familiar with data frames and if they're familiar with join-like
operations on those, we're there.  Hadley managed to move some people
in this direction with ggplot2, but I understand it's contentious.

>From Ben:

> I would prefer a syntax like
>
> parameters {
>   full_Data(Data);
> }
>
> to imply that complete_Data is of the same type and size as Data but with the missing values replaced by proposals.

I hadn't thought about higher-level syntactic features like
this --- that is, something that's not either a data type or
a function.  But there's no reason at all we couldn't do it
and it'd give us more flexibility.

>
> > transformed parameters{
> >   matrix[N,M] full_Data;
> >
> >   full_Data <- fill_missing_values(Data,missing_inds,missing_Data);
> > }

We'd probably have to do something like this, too, in transformed
parameters, but it could also be done at a higher level.

>
> This would work, although I think it puts an unnecessary burden on the user relative to full_Data(Data). Also, if we have placeholders in Data, I don't see why it would be necessary to pass missing_inds.
>
> Either way, continuous missing values can be managed but we also need ways to facilitate marginalizing out categorical missing values. To me, the easiest way to do that is to have placeholder values and change the behavior of the (non-count) PMFs to marginalize whenever they encounter a missing value.

This isn't right for all the marginalizations.  If I have a mixture,
then I can't just marginalize the discrete mixture indicator, I need
to get in the rest of it.  I'm not sure how to do that.

> To do a logit model this databasy way, the user would have to do
>
> data{
>   int N_obs;
>   int N_miss;
>   int K;
>   matrix[N_obs,K]  X_where_y_is_obs;
>   matrix[N_miss,K] X_where_y_is_miss;
>   int<lower=0,upper=1> y_obs[N_obs];
> }

This still looks like the NA approach to me.  What I was
thinking about is literally more database like with row and
column indices as columns --- like the dataframes you need
for ggplot2.  Here that'd be more like:

data {
  int<lower=0> N;  // num observed
  int<lower=1> I;  // num rows
  int<lower=1> J;  // num columns
  int<lower=1,upper=I> row[N];  // row for obs n
  int<lower=1,upper=J> col[N];  // col for obs n
  real val[N];                  // value for obs n

But my point was that we could abbreviate all of this somehow
(like say the way Ben suggested declaring parameters) and let
the user just input val with missing values on the input side.

Then you need to declare the parameters to be all the other
row/column combos, and then in transformed data the combination.

- Bob

On Wednesday, May 14, 2014 4:31:39 AM UTC-4, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> The one advantage of making the missing data values more explicit (and exposing the indices) is the ability to place priors on the missing data variables.  I don't work with models like this so I'm not sure how common of a use case this would be, but it seems plausible.

It should be more common than it is. But usually what could be considered a prior on a missing value is really a part of what Rubin calls the complete-data likelihood. So if you have a row vector like

2.4, NA, 7.3, 8.6, NA, NA, 1.9, ...

then it is a bit tortuous to consider 2.4, 7.3, 8.6, and 1.9 to be fixed while the NAs are unknowns to estimate. Rather you need a likelihood function for the whole vector, inclusive of NAs, and explicitly or implicitly integrate out the unknown values. For continuous unknowns, I think it is easiest to estimate them as part of the joint posterior and ignore those margins if you don't care about them. But for discrete unknowns, since Stan can't elegantly deal with them anyway, I think it is best to marginalize them out.

> Automatic marginalization of discrete parameters is interesting.  It would require a large amount of work under the hood though.  In particular, representing and transferring missing values would require replacing the int type with a special "stan_int" structure which carries a present/missing flag and (probably) bounds.

Maybe. The PMFs already know the bounds for the variable as a whole, so to me the main obstacle is currently not being able to recognize NAs. Are you saying that the user should be able to specify that there is a zero probability of the unknown value taking some subset of values in the sample space for the variable? I guess to be fully Bayesian we would need to work toward that but I haven't seen a lot of papers doing that (perhaps because it would be awkward to program in whatever language).

Ben

> So, I wonder, would this flag be useful for testing with Jenkins?

Sounds like it.  Daniel?

> Which makes the operator vec[n] of std::vector check if n is in the bounds of vec just like vec.at <http://vec.at>(n) does
>
> It turns out that this flag helped me catch this error:
>    to_matrix(const vector< vector<T> > & vec) {
>      vector<int> RC = dims(vec);
>      int R = RC[0];
>      int C = RC[1];
>      ...
>    }
>    to_matrix(some_empty_vector_of_vectors);

Where'd "some_empty_vector_of_vectors" come from?

> It seems that whenever vec is an empty vector, dims(vec)[1] doesn't exists, but this doesn't cause segmentation fault and the behavior of the function will be unexpected.

Right --- there aren't any further dims here.  We could probably
finesse dims() to fill out zeroes.

Nevertheless, this is not a good way to implement to_matrix because
of the unnecessary creation of RC.  Vectors aren't cheap to create,
destroy, or assign (at least prior to C++11), because they have mallocs
under the hood.

Why not just use this:

for (size_t i = 0; i < vec.size(); ++i)
  for (size_t j = 0; j < vec[i].size(); ++j)
    mat(i,j) = vec[i][j];

There's no way to get better memory locality because
mat will be organized column-maor and the vec of vecs
row major.

- Bob

is optimizing too strongly in the tail yielding a shorter step size than is necessary
in the bulk.  This can be remedied by tweaking the warmup adaptation window
sizes or the dual averaging parameters but it’s really hard to select something
that works better as a default.  If you warmup for longer you should see everything
converge to 0.8.

messages.body_plain:
> I do think that Stan should target people whose computer literacy is limited to Excel or Stata or SPSS or something, but trying to teach them just enough R or Python or Matlab to be able to use RStan or PyStan or MStan is not a good way to target them. We
> need to be giving them models that they can run from a web browser without compiling, can see the print output in the web browser, and read the .csv files into whatever program they know how to use.

I agree.

We'll be taking on Stata over the next couple of
years with Sophia Rabe-Hesketh.   The plan is to provide a bunch of
pre-built education models.

No plans for Excel or SPSS yet.

> Hopefully, that will get them hooked enough to where they are willing to learn how to write their own Stan models and compile them.

That'd be nice for a core (R/Py/Cmd)Stan audience.

It'd be great if we could give them a stepping stone that's more
like an iPython Notebook interface than having to install RStan.  But
I have no idea how we'd compile the models.

Cutting out the installation's not to be underestimated --- I have
to believe we still lose lots of users out of frustration at that step
judging from the e-mail we do get.

We may also want to consider permanently supporting the users who
are never going to want to define their own models in Stan (or for
bglmer() or for BUGS).

> Today, we could have dozens of popular Stan models running in any web browser by translating the C++ file to javascript with emscripten or compiling the C++ to PNaCL format which will run in Chrome. But we don't have a WebStan interface and don't have any plan to develop one, even though it would be simpler than the interfaces we have already written because WebStan would basically just be a wrapper around CmdStan.

Sounds like you do have a plan!  Let's find someone to do it.
If we can fit models client side, that'd be awesome.  I hadn't
wanted to build server-side web apps until we had a way to pay for
hosting.

- Bob

Hi all,

So, I now understand why we have duplicate error checking code.

The original stuff was in:
src/stan/math/error_handling/check_*
src/stan/math/error_handling/matrix/check_*

New stuff was implemented in:
src/stan/math/validate_*
src/stan/math/matrix/validate_*

I'm finding out that the order of header includes for the check_* functions matters a lot. This shouldn't be the case, but it's true now. What ends up happening is that things stop compiling by bringing in an additional header.

I'm going to suggest we reimplement all of our error handling. (By we, I mean I am volunteering and will take anyone else's time if you've got it.) I want to address:
- issue #665 - consolidating error handling code: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/655
- issue #640 - eliminate error message when sampling
- untangling this header mess
- simplify error handling by decoupling our error handling from Boost's complex, policy-based error handling.

Fortunately, all the original error handling code has unit tests, so it's easy to validate that the new error handling is the same. Unfortunately, none of the new error handling has any tests, so it'll take a little more time to implement safely than if it all had tests in place.

The biggest design change will be to decouple from Boost's style of error handling. I don't think this is an issue, but here's a list of pros and cons:

Pros:
- much simpler code
- easier to include a single error handling function
- removes the "Error in:" message that Boost provides
- we'd have much more control over error messages
- it'll be a lot easier to break apart our auto-diff library in the future if this section isn't tied into the traits.

Cons:
- no ability to flexibility change behavior, at least for the first incarnation (Note: we don't EVER use this functionality)

Anyone oppose? Anyone want to help? Time estimate -- if I start now, good chance I knock this out by tomorrow's meeting. ~30 existing error check functions with tests, which should take a handful of hours (hopefully under 5 hours). ~15 new functions without tests -- this will eat up a lot of time. Yesterday, I spent about 8 hours moving 3 of them to our existing error check functions. (Anyone that thinks that unit tests don't matter for "trivial" bits of code, they do. It helps make changes like this a lot easier to do.)

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] acceptance rates vs. target
messages.body_plain:
We need to separate out a few issues.

Firstly, the adaptation works fine one models we know HMC should fit, with the target
value of 0.8 quickly achieved.

Secondly, we can’t expect that success to carry over to all of the BUGS models, most
of which break every MCMC algorithm out there.  With the nominal parameterizations
none of these are going to be geometrically ergodic and adaptation will be brittle as
a consequence.  For example, step sizes that yield an average acceptance probability
of 0.8 in the bulk may cause way too many divergences in the tail (which we treat as
rejections, and hence skew the acceptance probability).  The flip size are cases
where adaptation goes crazy during warmup (as is common without geometric
ergodicity) and the acceptance probability vanishes.

Before worrying about the adaptation we have to worry about the well-posedness
of all of these models.  They need to be reparameterized and checked for heavy
tails (a la the HMC for hierarchical models paper).  Once we know they fit then
we can see if the adaptation is still causing problems.

> Now I'm worried (and maybe I should've been all along).

Most people don’t take geometric ergodicity seriously, but it’s
a big deal in practice and manifests as all of these pathologies
we keep seeing when people take careful looks at their models.

> I think this means we need to radically rethink our manual.
> We do not want to be providing example models (translations of
> BUGS models or otherwise), which should not be used.

I agree — but it’s hard to abandon them completely.  Will users
be content when we say “BUGS/JAGS has never been fitting these
well, you just never had the diagnostics to see it”?  Or, “we’ve
rewritten these examples so only compare these and ignore all
of the others”?

> And when you say won't fit, what's going to go wrong in terms
> of sampling?  Are we not going to be sampling from the posterior or
> is it going to be so slow that the effect is the same?

It depends on your perspective.  These algorithms are all ergodic,
just not geometrically ergodic.  Technically this means that they will
eventually explore the entire posterior BUT we no longer have the
Monte Carlo Central Limit Theorem so the accuracy of the Monte
Carlo estimates is unknown.  For example, biases estimates
of hyperparameter means, as we see in hierarchical models.

Agreed Daniel, this issue definitely deserves it's own thread.

I agree that template-based checking would be best.  It's a somewhat delicate problem though with a number of use-cases and desired behaviours.

In the case of the CAR models, because of the use of the precision matrix and the fact that one of the matrices is constant (i.e., it's data) we don't actually ever *need* it's Cholesky factor unless someone wants the normalizing constant.  However, to be pedantic, we need to always check that it's SPD and the most efficient way to do that is with the Cholesky factorization.  For cases like this (i.e., data parameters) what we'd really like is behaviour where it's confirmed to satisfy the constraints once and then never again.  (My memory is hazy, but I believe the CAR model is further complicated because the matrix is only positive semi-definite, but lets ignore that for now.)

Non-constant parameters should always be checked at every iteration regardless of compilation flags though because sampling can drive them into bad spaces.  Turning of checks in these cases will result in invalid samples.

On the other hand, bound checks have a non-trivial cost in some models (I've seen them pop up while profiling) and can often times be turned off.  These may be the kind of thing to turn off by a compiler flag for adventurous users.

I suggest that we try to concretely define a few desired use-cases for toggling error checking.  There is more than one and a solution for one may not work for another.  (Of course, on the flip side, solving all of them may be prohibitively complex...)

Cheers,
Marcus

With call-by-call control, maybe the user could
use a no-check argument or we could introduce something
like template parameters.  I've already been thinking about
this kind of syntax to start controlling up-to-a-proportion
or not behavior, which should be user controllable.

More inline below.

On May 24, 2014, at 1:49 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Friday, May 23, 2014 4:32:43 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> First off, I'll start with my stance. I don't think turning off all error checking with a single switch is a good thing. It may save time, but I'm not convinced Stan will work properly. The error handling is actually embedded deep within transforms and other things. With that said, I think the proper way to do it is not within the check_* functions themselves, but give the control to the caller. I think it makes sense that we have at least two levels of checking, and maybe more. I haven't thought about it enough.
>
> Ben, by disabling the check_* functions altogether, we lose all the checks in transforms and data IO.
>
> Yes, that is what I was trying to achieve, even though the checks in data or transformed data would only be executed once. The checks in transformed parameters are called a lot and don't add much value; either you wrote the transformation correctly and it is guaranteed that the transformed parameter is valid or you didn't and you will probably get a NaNs.

There are potentially two checks done on a transformed parameter.

1.  The check at the end of the block to make sure it's
    defined properly.

2.  The check on whatever distribution it's fed into to
    make sure the argument's right.

It's that first one that won't get made if you don't include it
in the constraints.

>  Presumably someone would have first done the model with exceptions and checks and validations and only turned them off after they were satisfied that their code is correct.

There's a bit of an issue with random behavior.  The transformation
may be right, but in some cases (say some initializations), may underflow
or overflow.

But I think when that happens, you'll get a rejection just without any
kind of message, which is really the right behavior.

So I'm not sure this is really a problem.

> But even if they haven't, I personally don't care. They asked for a non-default behavior of no checks, so they deserve what they get. That said, I'm not too particular about how we go about it or if we offer levels of checking or what.

As I said before, I'm OK with daredevil mode for those who want it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Dealing with index out-of-bounds errors
messages.body_plain:
The behavior has always bothered me. When we access things out of bounds, it doesn't actually stop the program, but instead rejects the iteration. If it's deterministic, it'll reject a bunch of times in a row and kick out.

I guess I'm thinking that size matches shouldn't throw domain errors, but something else and that we should do something more sensible with that sort of error handling.

I also believe that's the type of error handling that can be safely turned off after you've verified everything works based on shape of matrices.

Thoughts?

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Dealing with index out-of-bounds errors
messages.body_plain:
On May 29, 2014, at 12:32 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> The behavior has always bothered me. When we access things out of bounds, it doesn't actually stop the program, but instead rejects the iteration. If it's deterministic, it'll reject a bunch of times in a row and kick out.
>
> I guess I'm thinking that size matches shouldn't throw domain errors, but something else and that we should do something more sensible with that sort of error handling.

We don't have many options --- we can (a) print error messages,
(b) reject proposals, or (c) stop the whole sampler.

I wouldn't be opposed to (c) for indexing errors.

> I also believe that's the type of error handling that can be safely turned off after you've verified everything works based on shape of matrices.

This is only safe in the strict sense if all branching (including
indexing) depends only on data.  I know Michael's been lobbying for
just that restriction as it removes a lot of potentially bad
non-continuous behavior.

- Bob
